PUC PROJECT NO. 58482

LARGE LOAD DEMAND § PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
MANAGEMENT SERVICE § OF TEXAS

BASE POWER COMPANY’S COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSAL FOR
PUBLICATION OF NEW §25.521

TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:
Base Power Company (Base) submits these comments and executive summary in
response to Commission Staff’s proposal for publication (PFP) on new 16 Texas Administrative

Code (TAC) §25.521 relating to Large Load Demand Management Service (LLDMS).

I. INTRODUCTION

Base’s priority for LLDMS, is to ensure that the design of the service remains flexible
enough to manage the emerging and novel set of reliability issues that will be introduced with the
interconnection of a substantial number of large loads to the ERCOT grid. Base urges the
Commission to avoid overly restrictive rule language that could hinder innovative third-party
partnerships with large loads aimed at achieving the LLDMS program’s objectives. For example,
in the event of an anticipated EEA due to capacity concerns, Base envisions a solution where a
large load could comply with a deployment request by partnering (in part or in full) with
aggregated distributed energy resources (ADERs) within the same load zone. Additionally, Base
sees benefit in this partnership extending to transmission emergency solutions, whereby ADER
capacity with congestion relieving benefits on identified constraints can assist in resolving a
significant risk of load shed. In fact, a recent study by Piq Energy (in partnership with Base) has
proven that strategically sited ADERs can resolve network constraints and unlock firm

withdrawal capacity for large loads.! Not only does this indicate that ADERs should be

' See Piq Energy’s Flexibility without Curtailment: Aggregate DER Dispatch to Support Additional Firm Large
Load Service study (Sep. 1, 2026), available at
https://www.piqenergy.com/research/piq-energy-base-power---flexibility-without-curtailment.pdf

 incorporated as an interconnection study tool in ERCOT’s Batch process, but this benefit can and
should be leveraged for real-time transmission emergencies within the context of this rule.
Distributed energy resources offer a distinct advantage over conventional generation and
transmission solutions, as they can be deployed more rapidly and cost-effectively.” Ultimately,
the design of these suggestions are best handled in the ERCOT stakeholder process, and that

opportunity should not be limited by the scope of this rule language.

II. RESPONSE TO QUESTIONS

Question |:

Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling entity
representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to deploy but is
subject to availability verification during the Large Load Demand Management Service
(LLDMS) obligation period. Should a large load customer that is available but not
ultimately instructed to deploy during the LLDMS obligation period be compensated
some percentage of the market clearing price for the large load customer's availability to
reduce demand during the LLDMS obligation period? If so, what is an appropriate
payment to the large load customer for their availability during the LLDMS obligation
period?

Response:

Large loads that participate in this program will be contemplating the costs associated
with expected curtailment when submitting offers to provide the service. This may include costs
that cover agreements with third-party providers, fuel needed for onsite generation, or lost
revenue associated with curtailment. If the final path of proposed § 25.521(f)(1)(c) eliminates the
opportunity to recover 75% of the market clearing price, the incentive to participate in this
voluntary program will diminish and the chances that ERCOT may have to resort to firm load

shed during emergency conditions will increase. As with all ancillary service or reliability

? See ADER progress update (Base has deployed over 250 megawatts in the past year, and installations are currently
tracking at a rate of 35 megawatts per month) (Aug. 11, 2026), available at
https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/08/12/2026-08-11-Base-Power-Company-ADER- Updates. pdf

BASE COMMENTS Page 2 of 9

 service programs in ERCOT, participants should be paid the market clearing price for the
service, however, ERCOT should establish strict payment claw back penalties should the
participant fail on availability or performance criteria. The defined Real-Time (RTM) settlement
statement timeline is already at an appropriate cadence to handle payments (i.e., the RTM Initial
statement is issued on the fifth Business Day after the Operating Day), and associated claw backs
(i.e., the RTM Final statement is issued on the 55" Business Day after the Operating Day and the
RTM True-Up statement is issued on the 180" Business Day after the Operating Day). Base

offers revisions to the PFP language below reflecting this point of view.

Question 2:

Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a calendar year.
What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

Response:

Base offers no opinion on the budget level for the program, however, the Commission
should direct ERCOT to periodically submit a request for information to operational large loads to
determine the universe of likely participants. This capacity information, coupled with a
probabilistic assessment of likely emergency events and the defined offer cap can assist in
tailoring an appropriate budget for the service. On the topic of the offer cap, Base would like to
raise concems with being overly prescriptive in the final rule. Proposed § 25.521(d)(3)(B)(v) sets
the offer cap at $5,000 per megawatt hour, and this suggests that the intention was to link the
value to the current high system-wide offer cap (HCAP). It is worth noting that the Commission is
currently receiving comments under Project No. 59550, Quinquennial Review of System-Wide
Offer Cap Program Under 16 TAC § 25.509(d). It is reasonable to assume that in a future periodic
review the Commission may determine that modifying the HCAP is necessary. If linkage is the

intention, the rule language should reference the defined term instead of a hard coded value.

BASE COMMENTS Page 3 of 9

 Question 3:

What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and how far in
advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?

Response:
The assessment timeline (i.¢., forward-looking on a monthly, weekly, and daily basis)
outlined in § 25.521(d)(1) coupled with a 24-hour potential deployment notice presents a

reasonable cadence to identify and respond to elevated risks.

Question 4:

Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If so, what
limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

Response:

ERCOT has recently informed the market about voltage ride through (VRT) issues that
operational large loads impose on the system. Base’s understanding is that ERCOT is actively
designing locational curtailment groups of these large loads to avoid transmission-related
emergencies. Curtailment of these groups would be executed through a manual process in
coordination with Transmission Operators (TO).? During reliability events, when time is of the
essence, it would be preferable for the ERCOT control room to use systems to manage reliability,
instead of relying on a series of phone calls and manual TO action to backstop curtailment
requests. Base expects LLDMS to be implemented like all other ancillary and reliability services
with systematic deployment instructions between ERCOT and large load participants, and these
systems should be leveraged to the greatest extent possible. Additionally, giving ERCOT
flexibility to use LLDMS as a tool to address novel and emerging transmission issues can allow
for innovative partnerships to be formed between third-party service providers and large load

entities to mitigate dependencies on the ERCOT grid during times of stress. Base would caution

3 See ERCOT’s Interim LL VRT Assessment Update (Jun. 19, 2026), available at
https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/06/18/LLWG_Interim-VRT-Assessment-Update_06192026.pdf

 the Commission against being overly prescriptive in the final rule on allowable
transmission-emergency procurement criteria to give ERCOT and stakeholders flexibility on
defining solutions for this rapidly developing concern. Base offers revisions to the PFP language

below reflecting this point of view.

Il. GENERAL COMMENTS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Transmission emergencies — TAC § 25.521(d)
The below revisions are submitted to allow ERCOT the flexibility to procure LLDMS for

a transmission emergency as defined in § 25.521(b)(4).

(d) Procurement. ERCOT may procure LLDMS from a large load customer on an as needed
basis to help prevent an anticipated EEA event due to an extreme weather condition_or

transmission emergency, or alleviate an actual EEA event due to an extreme weather

condition_or transmission emergency.

(1) Request for proposal. ERCOT may issue a request for proposal to large load
customers that are pre-qualified to participate in LLDMS:
(A) _ based on monthly probabilistic modeling that identifies an elevated risk
for an EEA or transmission emergency event in the modeled month;
(B) based on weekly weather forecasting or probabilistic _modeling that

identifies an elevated risk for an EEA or transmission emergency event

during the forecasted week;

(C) _ in advance of an anticipated EEA Level | event due to an extreme weather

condition or transmission emergency; or

BASE COMMENTS Page 5 of 9

 (D) during an EEA event due to an extreme weather condition or transmission

emergency.

Offer cap — § 25.521(d)(3)(B)

The PFP explicitly defines the offer cap for the service at $5,000 per megawatt hour. Base
offers no opinion on this value, but it appears as if the intention was to link this value to the
HCAP. Base suggests referencing a defined term instead of a hard coded value to allow for

flexibility if these values are updated by the Commission in the future.

Payments and charges — § 25.521(f)

In terms of payments, a participant in LLDMS should receive the market clearing price
for the service, regardless of deployment status. The proposed language in § 25.521(g)
effectively allows ERCOT to establish payment reduction criteria for a LLDMS participant that
does not comply with availability or performance standards. The current ERCOT settlement
statement timeline currently allows for adjustments to payments and charges based on more
refined input data as it becomes available (i.e., each Operating Day is resettled at least three
times over the course of 180 days while accounting for refinement of metered data). It is
reasonable for LLDMS to leverage existing settlement functionality and timelines to make full
payments to participants on the RTM Initial statements, and institute necessary claw backs of
these payments on subsequent statements (i.e., RTM Final or RTM True-Up) if availability or

performance is lacking. Base offers the following revisions to reflect this point of view.

(f) Payments and charges.

BASE COMMENTS Page 6 of 9

 (1) ERCOT must pay a QSE that represents a large load customer participating in
LLDMS as follows:
(A) all payments must be based on a single clearing price;

(B) payments can be adjusted on the ERCOT settlement timeline as awards

prust—be—settted—monthhy_after—availability data is confirmed_and

performance criteria are reviewed;

(CB) A QSE representing a large load customer that deploys consistent with

ERCOT instructions during the LLDMS obligation period may receive
payment based on 100% of the market clearing price associated with the

deployed capacity.

IV. CONCLUSION

Base appreciates the Commission’s consideration of these comments.
